value: 0.025 to 0.067 (spatial resolution 15 to 40 deg as grating period, depending on the assumed contrast sensitivity)
method: behavioural: attraction of walking animals to dark targets of differing angular size (dual bars and piecewise sine gratings), combined with 3D reconstruction, optics and modelling
conditions: adults of 22 to 41 mm body length collected from decomposing logs in Tallaganda State Forest, kept individually at 19 C under 12 h:12 h light:dark; tested in the night phase in an otherwise dark room lit by a 100 W bulb above a diffuser (1.79e14 photons/cm2/s); one of 52 animals excluded for not responding to bright light, one used for reconstruction, 50 tested; 343 trials, 21 to 27 per stimulus including 23 controls; animals contributed one trial per experiment except for the two smaller bar targets, assessed up to four times (correction 10.1242/jeb.186551, which says the conclusions are unchanged); piecewise sine targets had the same average luminance as the background; controls showed no orientation (Watson U2 = 0.06, P > 0.10); targets of 10 deg and wider attracted the animals, 6.7 deg and narrower did not; the range comes from combining this threshold with optical modelling under assumed contrast sensitivities of 5 to 20

source.authors: Kirwan JD, Graf J, Smolka J, Mayer G, Henze MJ, Nilsson D-E
source.title: Low resolution vision in a velvet worm (Onychophora)

quote: Depending on the assumed contrast sensitivity of the animals, we estimate the spatial resolution to be in the range 15–40 deg.
note: The paper gives spatial resolution in degrees as the period of a sine grating ('conventionally given as the period of a sine wave'), so cycles/degree = 1/period: 1/40 = 0.025, 1/15 = 0.067 (computed, hence grade i). Same paper's abstract: the animals cannot spot or visually identify prey or conspecifics beyond a few centimetres. Read on the publisher's own free PDF (cob.silverchair.com), which carries the Company of Biologists copyright line only; Crossref registers the Company of Biologists user licence (not CC) for the accepted manuscript. Printed citation line: Journal of Experimental Biology (2018) 221, jeb175802; issue 11 appears only in the publisher URL path. Euperipatoides rowelli has a modelled acuity_cpd row on main (0.11, frontal acute zone, ray tracing of one eye; 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008808); this row is the behavioural estimate for the animal and is lower. The Kirwan 2018 Lund thesis row on main (Metazoa, flagged_unchecked) gives 20 to 30 deg for the velvet worm in its note.

value: males showed no significant preference for the conspecific electric playback in conditions I to IV (a null for species recognition by electric signals alone); the authors infer, without testing, that males use other, non-electric cues
method: behavioural playback of electric organ discharge (EOD) waveforms paired with conspecific, heterospecific or scrambled pulse-interval sequences (five conditions); time near each playback electrode scored from infrared video as strength of preference
conditions: 10 sexually mature males of this species; five playback conditions, amplitude-matched to a live fish at 52 cm; no preference in I (p = 0.130), II (p = 0.305), III (p = 0.346) or IV (p = 0.145); in condition V males favoured the heterospecific C. compressirostris signal, only marginally (p = 0.049), which the authors suggest may be a type I error; no differences across conditions (ANOVA p > 0.100); the authors state that the lack of preference is not per se evidence that the species cannot discriminate con- and heterospecific signals; no non-electric cue was tested. C. compressirostris tested with the same design.

source.authors: Nagel R, Kirschbaum F, Hofmann V, Engelmann J, Tiedemann R
source.title: Electric pulse characteristics can enable species recognition in African weakly electric fish species

quote: While the EOD waveform and SPI were both necessary and sufficient for species recognition in C. compressirostris males, C. tamandua males apparently utilize other, non-electric modalities.
note: CC BY 4.0 on the nature.com page and in Crossref. Quote, sample sizes, stimuli and Results read on nature.com. The 'non-electric modalities' clause of the quote is the authors' interpretation of a null, not a measurement. The same sentence supports both species rows; they are two findings (one per species).

value: five of the eight species detected 50 to 3600 Hz
method: auditory evoked potentials (AEP) to 50 ms tone bursts at 15 frequencies from 50 to 4000 Hz from an underwater speaker in a soundproof chamber; unanaesthetised fish held in a harness with subdermal needle electrodes
conditions: eight species: Piaractus brachypomus n=10, Metynnis lippincottianus n=10, Myloplus rubripinnis n=3, Myleus schomburgkii n=8, Serrasalmus elongatus n=5, S. spilopleura n=7, Pygocentrus nattereri n=10, P. piraya n=5 (55 to 112 mm standard length); aquaria at 26 +/- 1 C, 12 h light:dark; the species are not named in the sentence, so the row is graded as a family; the paper's Discussion places all eight species' best sensitivity at low frequencies (50 to 900 Hz) and the abstract says only slight threshold differences were found; of the other three species, Serrasalmus elongatus detected up to 3300 Hz and Myloplus rubripinnis and Pygocentrus piraya up to 3000 Hz; tones from 50 to 4000 Hz at up to 164 dB re 1 µPa in 6 dB steps; threshold = lowest level with AEP peaks at least 3 dB above background; sound pressure only, particle motion not measured; no anaesthetic

source.authors: Mélotte G, Parmentier E, Michel C, Herrel A, Boyle K
source.title: Hearing capacities and morphology of the auditory system in Serrasalmidae (Teleostei: Otophysi)

quote: Five species out of eight were able to detect frequencies ranging from 50 to 3600 Hz (Fig. 2).
note: CC BY 4.0 per Crossref. Methods and quote read on the nature.com page through the fetch tool (Table 1 per-species values were not returned). Pygocentrus nattereri was more sensitive than Piaractus brachypomus at 300, 900, 1200, 1500, 1800, 2100 and 2400 Hz (P ≤ 0.001), by over 27 dB SPL at 1200 Hz. Species-level hearing ranges need Table 1.
